system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2181-02-04 18:48:00 to 2181-02-05 17:38:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A female patient with end-stage renal disease, antiphospholipid syndrome, and a history of failed kidney transplant was admitted for worsening dyspnea and fatigue due to acute diastolic heart failure from volume overload. She was 5 kg above her dry weight, with bilateral pleural effusions and pulmonary edema confirmed on CT, but no pulmonary embolism. She underwent aggressive ultrafiltration via dialysis, leading to clinical improvement. She also had a non-functional left AV fistula with central occlusion, which was ligated successfully. Her warfarin was held perioperatively and resumed at discharge with a therapeutic INR of 1.7. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to monitor weight, continue dialysis, and follow up with surgery and her primary team.
problems: Other complications due to renal dialysis device, implant, and graft
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I’ve been reviewing your case. You came in today because of fatigue and trouble breathing, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. I woke up feeling so tired, I had to take a nap. When I woke up, my legs felt weak, like they’d give out. And I’ve been short of breath when I walk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You also mentioned some brief chest pains and thought it might be high potassium again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had that before. Weakness, fatigue—same feeling. I didn’t go to dialysis today because I came here instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was the right call. Your potassium came back at 6.3, which is high, especially with your kidney disease. But your EKG looks stable—no dangerous changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I feel so weak? Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be if it stays high, but we’re already treating it. You got albuterol to help shift potassium into your cells, and you’re now on dialysis to remove the excess. That should fix it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I also had some belly pain and loose stools the last couple days. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted that. No fever or serious signs, so it’s likely mild. We’ll keep an eye on it, but it doesn’t seem to be the main issue right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows some fluid in the lungs—mild pulmonary edema. That’s likely why you’re short of breath. It’s due to fluid buildup, which dialysis will help clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not my heart? Or a clot?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of a heart attack or pulmonary embolism. Your oxygen levels are good, and no tachycardia. This looks like fluid overload from your kidneys not keeping up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are much better. Potassium is now 4.7, and your acid levels have normalized after dialysis. You’re feeling less short of breath, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I feel a bit better. Still tired, but not struggling to breathe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Your lungs are clearing. One thing—we noticed your INR was low at 1.4. You’re on warfarin for your clotting condition, so we gave an extra 2 mg last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe? I don’t want to bleed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a small adjustment. We’re bringing it back to target. You’ll take an extra 1.5 mg tonight, then continue your regular dose. Your nephrologist will check it at your next dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re clearing you to go home. Keep up with your dialysis schedule, watch for swelling or breathing trouble, and take that extra warfarin dose tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my stomach issues and chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The chest pain has resolved and wasn’t cardiac. Likely related to your GERD, which your doctors are already evaluating. Continue your omeprazole and ranitidine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about sevelamer? I usually skip it because it makes my stomach worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping it on your list, but we understand. Talk to your nephrologist about alternatives if it’s too hard to tolerate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my eye drops and other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue all your usual medications—lamotrigine, trazodone, eye drops, blood pressure meds. Everything’s listed in your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ll follow up with my doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call if you have trouble breathing, chest pain, or any unusual bleeding. Otherwise, see you at your next dialysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Take care, and we’ll see your team at follow-up.

summary.summary_paragraph: A female patient with end-stage renal disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, and antiphospholipid syndrome was admitted for acute dyspnea and profound fatigue. She presented with symptoms concerning for hyperkalemia, including generalized weakness and exertional dyspnea. Labs confirmed hyperkalemia (K 6.3) and metabolic acidosis, and imaging revealed mild pulmonary edema due to fluid overload. She underwent emergent hemodialysis with successful correction of electrolyte abnormalities and symptomatic improvement. Her subtherapeutic INR (1.4) was addressed with a supplemental warfarin dose, and she was advised to continue her home medications, including those for GERD and dry eyes. She was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to maintain dialysis, monitor symptoms, and follow up for INR monitoring.
